utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please stand up and make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could I get the assistance for the ELMO to be lowered a little bit or -- not -- thank you. Okay. If you could please, sir, tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: My name is Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: S-a-l-a-p-u-r-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Now, I want to get right into the subject matter. So in July 1995 were you a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what position you held.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Head of administration for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please tell us a little bit about that position that you held. What did it entail?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That position involved work on the organisation and gathering of intelligence within the Army of Republika Srpska on the enemy and only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as part of your position, did you have a large staff working for you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You indicated that you were in the Main Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who was your immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the chief of sector, and at the same time assistant commander for intelligence and security Major General Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just so we're clear here because you said he was the assistant commander for security and intelligence, would Mr. -- would General Tolimir also be the immediate superior officer for Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And above General Tolimir, what was the next level?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who would be the commander back in 1995 in July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you engaged in the activities surrounding Srebrenica? And I'm speaking of a period sometime from July 6th to the -- July 11th when Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. In late June, between the 20th and the 25th, I went to Banja Luka for treatment. I was on sick leave, and I was supposed to stay there for a month. And after my recovery, I was supposed to work on the coordination and focal gathering of information concerning preparations for the attack on the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I was not aware of our activities before I learned about them in the media as far as our side is concerned. I arrived on that territory on the 13th, but I was not engaged in any related tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me stop you here for a second. How long had you been on sick leave, from what period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly when it was now. It was somewhere between the 20th and the 25th. I was supposed to be away for a month with the approval of my superior, General Tolimir. However, in view of the tasks that I was assigned and certain information that I was supposed to receive on the 12th of July in Belgrade, I cut my sick leave short and went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And very briefly, could you tell us what information you were trying or you were expected to receive on the 12th of July in Belgrade, with respect to which area, which location.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That information regarded preparations that were going on on the part of the Croatian army for an attack on the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you get that information when you went to Belgrade on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, including the exact date of the attack, the force of the attack, and the axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just so we don't go into it in great detail, the information that you received did that prove to be accurate or correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, only the date of commencement was shifted by two or three days in relation to the date that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in light of getting this information from your contact person that you met in Belgrade, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Acting from Bijeljina, I tried to get General Tolimir on the phone; however, I didn't succeed. I wanted to give him a brief summary of that information on the phone. Then I tried to contact General Mladic, but I was told from the Main Staff that they do not have direct contact with him either because he was in the area of Srebrenica. That was on the 12th, in the evening. I tried again early the next morning, the morning of the 13th, but since I didn't succeed and the information that I had was very urgent and important, I decided not to go on to Banja Luka but to go to Han Pijesak instead and look for either General Mladic or General Tolimir and advise him of the details of the forthcoming action in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And let me stop you here and just to clarify one point before we go on, your contact in Belgrade, was he from Belgrade? Was this a Serbian contact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To foundation. All the talk of contact has only been from the questions that Mr. Karnavas is asking. If the witness could explain if there is a contact at all. The way the questions are coming out Mr. Karnavas is providing the information in a leading way. I know he's probably just trying to facilitate it. But "contact in Belgrade" would be best coming out of the mouth of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How did you know to go to Belgrade on July 12th? Because you told us you were convalescent and then you went to Belgrade on the 12th. Now did you know go there, number one? What was the purpose? And number three, with whom did you meet? Don't tell us the person's name but in general what this person was.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I told you, I was recovering and I had problems with my spine. More exactly, lumbar sciatica. I also had acute ulcer problems on the large curve of my intestinal tract, that is the reason I was on sick leave. But I was constantly in contact with people from my service and I monitored the information that was available. They either brought it to my home or I went to the office in Banja Luka. On the 10th or the 11th, they received information about this meeting. And on the 12th in the morning, I went to Belgrade to attend the meeting. That person in question is a contact, a liaison who is not from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to clarify that point. Now, you told us you were trying to track down General Mladic on the 12th. And then I believe you indicated on the 13th you were heading towards Han Pijesak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the morning. And you were -- if I remember correctly, you were in Bijeljina at the time that you were placing these phone calls or trying to make these contacts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if you could please tell us what you did on that particular day, the 13th, step by step.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I arrived from Banja Luka, together with two other officers, information specialists, software specialists who were supposed to work on various programmes in Han Pijesak. They were supposed to take another car. But since I was unable to find either General Tolimir or General Mladic on the phone, I decided to go and find them in person. I cannot tell you exactly what time it was when we arrived. It's -- it was a long time ago. But we arrived in Konjevic Polje, more precisely, Kasaba. And there I stopped by the command of the Protection Regiment - I believe it was the military police battalion - to see one of the officers and find out how I can get in touch with either General Mladic or General Tolimir, because I thought the military police should know. They explained to me that Tolimir was somewhere in the area of Zepa, while General Mladic was in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you here for a second, just so we can orient everybody here where Kasaba is. From Bijeljina, as you would travel, you would be heading towards Zvornik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then the next location after Zvornik would be the intersection of Konjevic Polje? And then if you were to take a left on the road, that would take you towards Bratunac, but if you went straight --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if you went straight --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then you were on your way towards Vlasenica when you stopped in Kasaba. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: In Kasaba, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you recall who it was exactly that you met in Kasaba when you got this information that General Mladic was I believe you said in Bratunac or Srebrenica -- Bratunac you said.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I cannot recall precisely whether it was the duty operations officer or somebody else's, well, a commander or somebody, those are details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the approximate time when you would have reached that location?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I can't tell you the time exactly. I attempted to get him on the phone at 7.00, the time it took to get ready. It could have been 9.00, maybe 10.00, 11.00, that range.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me show you what is marked as D197 for identification, 197/1. And perhaps we can put the -- do we have one for the ELMO? We do, yes. You may want to keep your glasses handy, because I'm going to be going through some documents with you. Now, this is a document provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution, and this is purported to be an intercept and it has your name there. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it also makes reference to a Major Malinic, the commander of the 65th Protective Motorised Regiment Armoured Battalion. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, first of all do you know -- what are we talking about when it says here the 65th Protective Motorised Regiment? What is that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That is the protective regiment of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are they like military police for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: They had within their structure a battalion of the military police and some other units, whether it was an armoured battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: -- or something else. But anyway, these are units providing protection and security for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would it be fair to say that this is a Main Staff asset? It belongs to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us under which unit, which sector, was the 65th Protective Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It was a unit directly under the Main Staff under the command of the chief of staff. It had its peculiarities, because the battalion of the military police is under the command of a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you know Major Malinic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, it says here according to this intercept that it's 13 July at approximately 10.15 in the morning. Would that be about the time that you were at that area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall whether you saw on that particular day when you were at Kasaba, Major Malinic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Whether it was Malinic or some other officer, I could not tell you with any degree of certainty, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it says here. It says: "Pero Salapura," Pero is not your first name is, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, Petar, but they call me Pero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it says: "VRS security service," but that's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it also states here that there were some prisoners that were at the football field in Kasaba, about 500 of them. Do you recall whether you noticed them when you stopped there on that particular morning?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Whether it was the football pitch in Kasaba or Konjevic Polje, I don't know. It's on the right when you go from Zvornik along the road, but that's not where I stopped. I went straight to the command. Yes, there were prisoners there, quite a lot. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know what they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Nothing. They were sitting. They were gathered there. Guards were around them. Our soldiers were standing guard. Some of them were standing, others were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of those particular prisoners, at that particular location, on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long you were in Kasaba or in that area.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but not long. Just the time it took for me to get that information. So much time has elapsed, I cannot give you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, once you received that information, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I returned to Bratunac and then -- sorry, there at the brigade command I looked for General Mladic, and I was told he was in Srebrenica. So I went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it says you returned, you actually turned back -- went backwards?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. I went back to the turn-off for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you at any point in time locate General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, in Srebrenica, when I got there. I don't know whether it was soldiers or policemen, some troops told me he was in the building of the town hall or somewhere where he was giving an interview. There were some TV crews and a group of officers around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in order to get to Srebrenica you would have to go -- at least one way would be through Potocari. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you go to Potocari or through Potocari on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you stop in Potocari at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, where was it that you learned that General Mladic was in Srebrenica as opposed to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: In Bratunac I was told he was in Srebrenica. I passed through Potocari and went on to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you passed through Potocari, did you at any point in time see Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. At that time I didn't even know he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you know Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm going to reserve that topic for later on. We'll get to Colonel Jankovic. But now let's stay with Mladic in Srebrenica. Do you recall about what time it was when you got to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know. It's difficult to determine now how long the road to -- I believe I didn't stay very long in Bratunac. And I left the two officers who had come with me there to have lunch. I don't know how long it took. It could have been until noon. It's really very difficult to give you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it when you got to Srebrenica you found General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you speak with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was giving an interview. I came close at a distance of several metres from where he was standing. He noticed me and he gave me a sign with his hand to stop right there and wait. I'm not sure how much longer it took. He came up to me and we greeted each other. He asked me what I was doing there. I started to tell him about how the preparations were going, the time frame, and the Croatian forces that were preparing for an attack against the Republika Srpska Krajina. He told me to cut the story short by interrupting me all the time by says: "And? Yes, yes. And?" So I proposed as for that replacement, the marginal involvement of the Main Staff in that territory to be terminated as soon as possible and that I should get involved with the preparations and planning of the activities to be undertaken by the Army of Republika Srpska in the western section, defensive actions. There was a possibility that as many as 30 kilometres of totally undefended front line could open up there. He was probably still enthusiastic from the success of that operation and from talking to the journalists. My report was a bit of an embarrassment, to put it that way. He raised his voice and he shouted at me. He said that what I was saying was not true, something along these lines, that I was exaggerating, that I was a doom merchant, and that it was not for me to propose what should be done, that he would be the one to call that particular shot, that sort of thing. I was probably a little angry on account of his reaction. I was still quite ill, after all. So I said goodbye to him and I turned back. I went back to the car and drove back to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you here and let me clear up a point. A little bit earlier, I'm not clear, were you to get involved or was somebody else to get involved in the preparation, in setting up the defensive line of this territory where you said it was some 30 kilometres that was undefended?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That's the western part of Republika Srpska, the line towards the Republic of Serbia and Krajina, not 30, 300. The Main Staff and the commander based on all this information were to carry out a swift assessment and take a decision as to what should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Because there was very little time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just -- if we could just fast-forward a little bit in time. Could you please tell us whether this -- these activities occurred, and if so what were the results of those activities that you had learned, that is, the attack that was about to ensue from that area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, the operations took place in early August. The Army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, to the best of my recollection, very soon, three days later, started their withdrawal. We were ill-prepared and we started late to transfer our forces into that section. So that's what happened. Large sections of the front remained undefended. Units were gathered or parts of units were gathered from different formations. And very soon, the front line started breaking up. Therefore, the whole western section of Republika Srpska was at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said you went back to Han Pijesak. Could you please tell us whether you stopped anywhere from Srebrenica to Han Pijesak on that particular day, and I believe we're speaking of the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about what time it would have been when you arrived in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know. It was sometime in the afternoon. It's difficult for me to say now what time exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us why you went to Han Pijesak. What's there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I had those two officers with me, the IT experts who were supposed to install a unique programme for the benefit of the administration, the centre itself and all its institutions. I was supposed to leave them there and return immediately to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why were you to return to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was supposed to get on with my treatment and continue to monitor these activities in as far as that was possible. But the journey had been quite long and I was on painkillers, so I was suffering severe pain and I stayed there and spent the night there in Han Pijesak. I couldn't continue the journey immediately on account of the pain that I was suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that would have been the night of the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: 13th, yes. The 13th and the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's where the Main Staff is, correct, Han Pijesak? The headquarters of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. That is where the headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where did you stay in Han Pijesak? Did you have any quarters yourself, sleeping quarters?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I had a room, a small room, to sleep in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when did you leave Han Pijesak to go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I afraid I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated you spent the night in Han Pijesak and you had planned to go to Banja Luka. Could you please tell us when. Was it the next day? Did you stay more days in Han Pijesak? When did you return to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The next day I was to return immediately, first thing in the morning. However, the duty officer or the duty operations officer, whoever, informed me that the road had been closed for all traffic moving from Vlasenica to Zvornik. One of my assistants knew about that. He had received the message, and he informed me that I could not travel, that I had to stay until further notice, stay put where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you can just sit back and relax. You don't have to lean forward to speak into the mike. It picks it up, so just relax, from where you are. All right. Now, why was the road closed again?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't know it then, because no other reason was given, no explanation. Probably there were units being moved about or prisoners of war being moved about. There was probably some kind of activity underway, some kind of activity I suppose. I didn't see any reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us how long did you have to wait there in Han Pijesak before you could leave.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I can't be sure about the date, whether it was the 17th, the day we received information that the road was now again open for traffic. I'm not sure if it was the 16th, the 17th, possibly the 18th. I came back on the 18th. That much I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if -- just to make sure that I'm clear. From the evening of the 13th to about some time in the 18th, you were in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go back to the 13th. When you got to Han Pijesak and you stayed there that night, the night of the 13th, the same night that you had returned from seeing Mladic in Srebrenica, do you recall whether you saw any high-ranking officers, higher-echelon officers, on that evening? Did you come into contact or see anyone?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I don't think there was anyone up there, with the exception of General Miletic, as far as higher-echelon officers were concerned. As for my own administration, there was a major and there was an ensign, a junior lieutenant. And what I was told was what the situation was like, that some people were on leave, that some people were up and about carrying out assignments. There were very few officers there at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During that period of time, did you have any contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see General Mladic? Did you see him walking about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, not after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Not after that. I don't know that he had arrived from that section. If he was there, he was probably sleeping in a different place, about 200 metres further into the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General Miletic, what was his position within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was the chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with General Miletic to find out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that General Tolimir who was your immediate superior officer was in Zepa or that's what you had heard. Did you see him at any point in time from the 13th in the 18th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. I failed -- I tried, but I failed to get through to him on the phone. There were no phone lines that were open to him. It was only he who picked up the phone himself. But during that period of time, he never did. I kept looking for him, because I was angry. I was angry that people had been involved in other assignments. One of our analysts was even allowed to go on leave during a time at which we faced so many difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you see Colonel Beara during those days?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He wasn't up there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, since we're on with Colonel Beara, you're intelligence; he's security. Did your two sectors interact, exchange information, work together?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: As for exchanging information, we did that. His section was sending information on to my section, because they had more men. They were a strong unit, section, and we were just a very small section of the staff. And they kept receiving much more intelligence than we did. My section did not have the information that they had, because we were not authorised to deal with that sort of information. Therefore, it was precious little that we could give them. Our relations were regular. General Tolimir coordinated all these relations, and everything went through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's been some testimony here with respect to how the security organ functioned. In particular, that - just to give an example - with respect to the mail, that the commanders of the brigades, for instance, could not open up the mail of the security officers, could not read the mail, and that the security officers could directly report on certain matters, especially if it was counter-intelligence, directly to their higher echelon. Did the intelligence organ operate in the same fashion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. The intelligence organ received information and sent it on to the chief of staff and the commander directly. It did not have the same level of protection, and this wasn't the kind of information that would be gathered in the same way as with the security service. The intelligence organ is attached to the staff. At its lower levels, it was subordinate to the chief of staff, and at the staff level through the sector directly to the commander. The commander ran the security organ directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The commander -- now, you're saying the commander at the brigade level ran the security organ or the commander at the Main Staff level? Are we speaking about security or are we speaking about intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: You asked me about both, so I provided both answers. Intelligence is related to the chief of staff. In principle, whichever bodies had an intelligence organ, an intelligence body, and the security service would be related to the commander. And that's the overall command structure. At the level of the Main Staff, there was a separate sector where both services were closely tied to the sector chiefs, in addition to which the security service had a direct link with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during that -- those days, I just want to make sure that we have a clear understanding, the 13th -- the evening of the 13th, the 14th, the 15th, the 16th, the 17th, all the way up to the 18th, did you have any contact with Mladic or Beara or anyone else while you were in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I did have contact probably with the officers who were over there. I don't know exactly. I believe only General Miletic was there. I don't seem to remember that there was anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time get involved with any of the activities after the fall of Srebrenica? And I'm talking about the 12th, the 13th, the 14th, anything dealing with the prisoners or men that were separated in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I didn't and the body that I was in charge of didn't either, because that was not part of our remit, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Nor did we have the necessary resources or forces or manpower. It simply wasn't within our remit. Our job was the other side, from the beginning to the very end of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to show you a document that has been marked as P507. It has already been admitted I'm told. P507. It's a notation. If you could please look at that. It says here: "14th July, Jokic." And underneath it, it says: "Colonel Salapura called - Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." All right. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Drago, do you know who they're talking about in this particular -- do you know who might this person be, Drago?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know and I can't remember what the whole thing is about, what the purpose is. Beara, Golic -- Golic was a major, Beara was a colonel and these two, I don't know. I can't remember what the whole thing was about or what the reason was behind it. This tells me nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's take it one step at a time. First I wanted to identify the people. Do you know who Drago is? Do you know who they might be referring to; yes, no, or maybe?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Beara, we're clear on him. Right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Golic, do you know who Golic is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I do. This is Golic, he was the assistant for intelligence with the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So he would have been in your sector, but at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you briefly touched on it and I was going to ask: Do you have any idea of what this is referring to? After all, it says -- has your name that you called. And then it says: "Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." In other words, these two individuals, one of who is a colonel in the security sector of the Main Staff, are to report to Golic of the intelligence sector within the Drina Corps. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no. I can't venture a guess. I don't see any inherent logic in it. That's what it says, but I don't know what the reason is. I don't think I can comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, please tell us why you don't see the inherent logic, so at least we can follow that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't see what I was to convey at the time or what the whole thing was about. I may have happened to be on the phone at the time. I had spent some time there, but I was in bed most of the time. I may have been at the room at this particular point in time. Maybe there was a message that was to be conveyed, but who from and who was the recipient? I can't make it out. I don't see any logic in it. Officially, if you look at the official channels, it just doesn't make sense. And I can't see any specific task as such. I can't link it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But because we're not in the military and we're --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It's possible that I did convey someone's orders but I really don't know now and I don't think I can comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just if you hear me out for one second, we're not in the military and we're trying to follow this and why it doesn't have any logical sense to you. Based on your last answer you said: "Officially, if you look at the official channels, it just doesn't make sense." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, these are two different services. Here you have a major and here you have a colonel. But as I said, I don't know what this is about. It's very difficult to think back and remember now. It's been nine years after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It was written down in a journal, but by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I'm not sure which journal this is an excerpt from. I'm sure that it's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, very briefly I told you earlier that we were going to discuss Colonel Jankovic. Perhaps you can tell us who he was at that time that is, because I understand he's still with us, that is, in the physical sense.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic was an analyst with the intelligence administration of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us as an analyst with the intelligence administration of the Main Staff what his functions were. And again, you don't have to lean forward. Just from there where you're sitting you can tell us, nice and gently.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I think he worked on processing and analysing information, monitoring the situation with regard to HVO units, Croatian Defence Council and Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he a commander in any sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. He was an analyst. He couldn't give orders to anyone, not even to himself, in the military sense of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But he was a colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But I mean, we all had this impression that colonels go around commanding and issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. He was with the intelligence administration. He had no subordinates. And we were fully staffed. I believe he was to have another three or four assistants, but he didn't have any. He was working by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So was he working by himself, is that what you're telling us, without a staff, analysing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. No, he was subordinated to himself or to no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who did he report to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He wrote briefs, reports, the results of his analysis that he submitted to the head of section for analysis, Karanovic, and to me when I was around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now just to make sure because I see we may need to make a correction, were you fully staffed or not fully staffed? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: What did you say? Did I have what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just check -- relax for a second. In my previous -- previously, it says here on the record that you were "fully staffed," you being the intelligence unit. And I want to make sure whether that's what your answer was. Was it that you were fully staffed, your intelligence unit, where Jankovic was working?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no. We had less than 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to correct that. Now, when we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think this might be a good time for us to take a break, Your Honour, because when we get back I would like to discuss what Colonel Jankovic was doing -- oh, I'm told I've discombobulated this new environment. Since we have all this time, as I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could tell us, first of all, we know that Colonel Jankovic was in Bratunac sometime in early July. Could you please tell us who issued him that order to go there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: When I arrived at the command post on the 13th, I was informed by Major Malinic, I think he was the man who made the report, that Colonel Jankovic had been designated and sent to the command of the Knin Corps [as interpreted] as liaison officer for UNPROFOR troops, or rather, the UNPROFOR base in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which corps was he sent to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I was worried there. Now, who was his immediate superior officer, Jankovic's, normal?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, at that time when I was not around, it was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But listen to my question, then we'll -- I'll take you back. Who was normally Colonel Jankovic's immediate supervisor? Who did he answer to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Karanovic, Lieutenant Colonel Karanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So a colonel was reporting to a lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in which sector was this Mr. -- Lieutenant Colonel Karanovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Head of section for analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And who did this Karanovic report to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: To me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've -- concretely speaking, did you order Jankovic, Colonel Jankovic, to go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't even there when he left. I was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When he did -- when the issue -- when the order was issued to Colonel Jankovic, were you informed of that order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, I was in Banja Luka. It was General Tolimir who was in command, who organised the work as head of sector in my absence. They did not need to inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know then who was the individual, who was the officer, that ordered Colonel Jankovic to go to Bratunac and be subordinated to the Drina Corps or attached? However -- whatever the precise terminology is.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who could have possibly -- given the universe of choices, who could have possibly issued that order to Colonel Jankovic, in light of his position and in light of where he was serving?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: General Tolimir, or the commander of the Main Staff in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you ever learn what Colonel Jankovic was doing in Bratunac at the time? Or let me put it this way: Who he was supposed to be doing when he first arrived? We'll take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. I was told when I arrived, because he was not around, that he had been designated to be the liaison officer with the UNPROFOR in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why would they need someone like him? Because as I understand it they already had Captain Momir Nikolic in Bratunac; why would they need Colonel Jankovic to come from Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know where Momir Nikolic was at that time. And I don't know -- I'm not aware anyway that Momir Nikolic was the liaison officer. Jankovic was in our forces the only officer who had a good command of the English language, and that must have been the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you ever learn whether his portfolio, if I could use that term, was expanded so he would have commanding powers while he was in Bratunac? In other words, did anyone make him a commander so that he could issue orders to command others below him, such as, for instance, Momir Nikolic, to just pick an example?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, I don't see why he would be. He was an analyst and he was designated to be the liaison officer. I don't see why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, after the events in Srebrenica, did you ever have an opportunity to speak with Colonel Jankovic and find out what exactly happened while he was there, Bratunac, Potocari, during those days?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I spoke to Colonel Jankovic, but only later when I saw him in Banja Luka after the Croatian offensive had already started. And then everybody from Han Pijesak came to Banja Luka. But I didn't speak to him at that time. At that time, we were pre-occupied with much more urgent problems and all the rest was forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were the problems you were speaking about with regard to the information you had received on the 12th of July of the ensuing attack?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But would it have been normal - I don't know, maybe you can help us out here - for Colonel Jankovic to make some sort of a report or give you some sort of an update as to what he was doing in your absence when he was subordinated to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's lots of assumptions in these leading questions, that this person is subordinated and other issues that are really Mr. Karnavas's developments and not the witness's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have asked a lot of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "The ensuing attack." I don't think there was an ensuing attack at that time. Perhaps you could ask the date of the attack and we could get down to business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The attack was coming and we know that it came, and it's a fact, he testified to it. He indicated that he was sent down to the corps. In the spirit of cooperation, I'll go about it in another way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And perhaps I could show you a document at this point in time and we'll touch upon this very issue. If I could show you what is Exhibit D164, a document provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution. We're not going to discuss it in detail; I just first want you to look at it. And you see it has a date on top of it, 13 July 1995. Do you see that, sir, the top, the date?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at the bottom on the right-hand it says: "14 July 1995, 0030." So that would be 30 minutes into July 14th. Do you see that, sir? You need to answer so we can make a record.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, just a couple more questions. And we're talking about the same Jankovic, Colonel Jankovic. Right? This was his first name, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, getting closer -- now, could you please tell us, Colonel Jankovic of the Main Staff security sector, to whom is he addressing this report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: We see from this that this report is addressed to the sector of the Main Staff, namely to General Tolimir, and the command of the Drina Corps, the intelligence section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so this -- and underneath we see it says here specifically: "To: Command of the Drina Corps intelligence department." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, why would he be making this report to the command of the Drina Corps intelligence department?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: To the command of the Drina Corps, section for intelligence. They settled it within the Drina Corps. I don't know who decided, the commander or somebody else decided how the communication would go to the base. I don't want to make any comments, but when he arrived the order was that all the information should be sent through the intelligence section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And to your knowledge at this point in time, was Colonel Jankovic working on behalf of the Main Staff in Bratunac, the Drina Corps, the Bratunac Brigade, or some other brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're working for all those units when you're working in the army, so without some specificity, it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, the full series of questions may be not proper to put to this witness, because we heard that this witness was there on -- only on the 17th of July. I don't know whether he's well informed about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour -- I said -- I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ever learn, did there ever come a time where you learned, to whom Colonel Jankovic was working for at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was informed, as I told you, when I arrived at the command post that he had been sent to the command of the Drina Corps as liaison officer with the UNPROFOR on behalf of the Drina Corps. And of course, he reported, as you can see here, to the intelligence section of the command. And it was up to him to decide whether it was necessary or not. What I have just told you is the way it functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This may be a good time to take the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm going to be asking you about the last paragraph when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, I believe we left off with document D164. In light of your position in the intelligence unit or sector, I would like you to focus on the last paragraph of Colonel Jankovic where it states: "I think that if we want to take over the enclaves of Zepa and Gorazde in the same way, it will be necessary to present the operation in Srebrenica in the media, so as to show that we had rendered adequate treatment to the civilians, and even to soldiers who surrendered their weapons." In light of your position and knowing Colonel Jankovic, could you please give us some explanations about this particular paragraph. What conclusions, if any, can you draw?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: You have a postscript down here and a personal opinion attached by Colonel Jankovic. At that point in time, this only seems logical, and it arises out of the position that he held at the time. Looking at this from the perspective of the presence of the international community as well as the public opinion, internationally speaking, concerning the overall picture in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially as regards Republika Srpska and its army. This is a recommendation and a desire that this unfavourable image that we enjoyed at the time be righted in a way. And the whole of this communique in terms of its contents speaks for itself and speaks with sufficient clarity as to what his tasks were and the problems that he encountered. It was about simple coordination liaising between the UNPROFOR forces and the corps command and here you have his personal view, representing an attempt to perhaps help in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had you seen such opinions expressed in the past in the sense that, for instance, someone like Colonel Jankovic would give a report and then attach as well his personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: In our organ we used to do this, because our job was of a peculiar nature in relation to the other staff organs as well as his own. Because our job was to deal with the enemy and the environment. Everything that was outside the territory under the control of Republika Srpska. Obviously we were interested in gathering information and we were interested in how the world saw the entire situation. This was frequently the case, namely, that analysts made proposals or submitted reports containing proposals and recommendations which were sent by the administration to other institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we've heard testimony that right about that time Colonel Beara was engaged in other activities and that the men that were separated and others that were captured were ultimately killed. In looking at that particular paragraph, the opinion expressed by Colonel Jankovic, an analyst with the intelligence department of the Main Staff, can you, based on looking at this, can you tell us whether you can make any conclusions, draw any conclusions, as to whether at the point in time when this was written Colonel Jankovic would have been aware of any activities ongoing by Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is extremely speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I had to ask it, Your Honour. I couldn't resist. Good objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go through some other documents briefly. I'll stick with this period in time. And I first want to talk to you about some information that has come to the attention of the Office of the Prosecution by one of -- by someone whom they've had numerous contacts with, someone by the name of Dragomir Vasic. And he has indicated in one of their statements -- one of his statements, I believe it's 10 June 2003, that it was on the 13th of July when Mladic ordered you to kill the prisoners. And he states, and I'm quoting from page 61, he states that you refused, that you went to Han Pijesak and you took a medical certificate. And then he said: "They started looking for Beara." So first of all, do you know this Mr. Vasic, Dragomir Vasic? Do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, I don't know who this person is. No, I don't remember. I don't believe I know this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just briefly interject. There is a suggestion in that question that Mr. Vasic is somehow an agent or a cooperator with the Office of the Prosecutor. And just for clarity, I want to make sure that the public knows that he is a target of an investigation; he is not a cooperator. People that are thought to be cooperators could be in potential danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I never suggested that -- I really don't understand what that last part was. The gentleman has met with the Prosecutor six times and has given him documents. So certainly somebody's cooperating with somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, Mr. Karnavas, all those statements concerning the relationship between that person and the Prosecution are totally irrelevant to your question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, but I haven't said anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you know -- I think I advised you many times, if not absolutely necessary, do not mention the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe you could do your job much better without mentioning the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It's very difficult with this particular statement, since it's to the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor elicited this information from the gentleman. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You could not -- have the relationship of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Getting back to where we were. First of all, did this ever occur, in other words did Mladic, General Mladic, order you on the 13th to kill all the prisoners as Vasic, Dragomir Vasic, told the Prosecutor on 10 June 2003? Did this ever occur?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: May I please add some clarifications? No, this is absolutely untrue. I told you at the outset that I did have a conversation with General Mladic, only a brief one. It only took several minutes. For me, it was a most unpleasant conversation and I said why. The conversation amounted to downgrading my own work by General Mladic. I don't think General Mladic would ever have ordered something like this to me personally, because my position, not only with regard to prisoners of war but in a more general sense, the position which I held from the very beginning of the war, was entirely in compliance with everything, as Jankovic said a humane treatment and respect for all conventions. In our rules of service, in our work, this is one of the key propositions, the Geneva Conventions. And I don't think that any intelligence officer would fail to comply with that. I do not know this person and I think this bit of information is completely untrue. I'm not sure why it was provided and what the intention was. It's -- it would have been absurd for me to take a rifle and go and do whatever he had in mind I would have -- there were other objectives there, perhaps, behind this statement. I'm not sure what General Vasic's intention was when he said that. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Vasic is not a General. Now --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, since -- let me ask you this: Has the Office of the Prosecution ever contacted you? We know Srebrenica occurred back in July 1995. Today it's nine years later. We're in June 2004. Have they ever contacted you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I believe it was in 2001 or 2002, team 9, I believe, if there is such a team. There was a lady, an American lady. The subject matter was Alija Izetbegovic and Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you speak to them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many times did they contact you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: This once and later they called me on my mobile phone, someone did, but also in relation to the conflict between Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did anyone from the Office of the Prosecution, in light of your position and in light of Colonel Jankovic's involvement or activities during the events in Srebrenica, did anyone from the Office of the Prosecution ever contact you to get any information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had they expressed an interest, would you have been willing to meet with them and provide them information or talk to them as you talked to team 9 who were interested in Naser Oric and the late Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I noticed no interest whatsoever on their part. I certainly would have been willing to talk to whoever was interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we talked a little bit about Jankovic. Now I want to talk to you about the 10th Sabotage Unit.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us to whom this asset belonged to.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The 10th Sabotage Detachment was a sabotage and reconnaissance unit. It was an independent unit attached to the Main Staff. Like all other independent units, it was directly subordinated to the commander. As for its professional use, as for training and anything like that, the intelligence organ would have been in charge. As for making proposals on how this unit was to be used for special tasks, the proposals would also be made by the intelligence organ, and then this proposal would be approved or ordered by the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so I'm clear, would you be the person in charge of the intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. I was the chief of intelligence and administration -- I used to be, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the whole world by now has heard of Erdemovic. Have you heard of this individual?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Everyone has.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you've heard about his activities, his killings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who ordered the 10th Sabotage Detachment to go to the Bratunac area during the events surrounding Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The 10th Sabotage Detachment, this is something that I verified later, was involved in combat operations in Srebrenica. It was subordinated to the command of the Drina Corps. After combat operations were completed, that was only the one half. And the other half was in the Modrica area. And I visited them when I was on my way to Belgrade. This half was subordinated to the command of the Drina Corps when the combat part of the operation was over. I'm not sure about the date, whether it was the 9th or the 10th when the units of the Army of Republika Srpska entered the town of Srebrenica itself. The corps commander issued instructions that a return to the base was possible. On their way back, an APC tumbled over and one soldier was killed. The detachment commander was injured. I believe there were two or three soldiers that were wounded in that accident. As for the rest of them, the remaining half, once they had returned to base, the detachment commander granted them ten days, or at least that's what they told me once I was back at the command post on the 13th, he granted them ten days' leave. On the evening of the 13th, I tried to get in touch with the detachment commander by phone, however, he was away receiving treatment for his injury. So I couldn't get through to him. But one of the soldiers did tell me -- I asked them what was going on, and they told me that all the soldiers were on leave apart from those providing security, the few soldiers who remained back at the base. And the other half were on a mission in the Modrica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here for a second. Let me go back to my original question. In very concrete fashion, just tell me if you know: Who was it that ordered the 10th Detachment -- the 10th Sabotage Detachment to be subordinated to the Drina Corps and go to the Srebrenica area during the events concerning Srebrenica back on July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I'm not sure who exactly issued the order to the commander at the time. It didn't strike me as very important. I was unable to get through to General Tolimir at the time, therefore I don't know who exactly gave the order, whether it was Tolimir or the commander directly, the commander of the Main Staff, or whether it was through General Tolimir or perhaps General Tolimir himself, but I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And is that the universe of choices as to who could issue an order to have this asset of the Main Staff subordinated to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: If we are looking at a combat task for which this unit was not meant to be used and the order on its establishment contained a clause that this unit would only be used for particular special tasks, and that all sort of non-special use was strictly forbidden. Therefore, the use of this unit for combat operations could only have been ordered by the commander of the Main Staff, since he was the one who signed the order. Therefore, he was the only one who could have had the authority to change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, prior to the events of Srebrenica, which has we've indicated commenced on July 6th, 1995, did you at any point in time make any recommendations as to the usage of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, since as I understand your testimony earlier, the head of the intelligence unit would be making those recommendations for the usage of that particular detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. On a number of different occasions, but only for reconnaissance- and sabotage-related tasks. Outside that, the chief had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But I'm speaking concretely for Srebrenica and that period around July 1995. Did you make any recommendations for their usage with respect to Srebrenica, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I wasn't even there when the unit got involved in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that on the 13th you were trying to get in touch with the commander who apparently was ill or injured. Who is that commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would this be --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Colonel, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would this --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it lieutenant colonel or is it lieutenant or is it colonel? Which of the three?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is -- was Lieutenant Pelemis the same commander that authorised the ten days of leave that you had learned of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it all of the information -- well, let me ask you -- after you heard about what had happened or Erdemovic had been involved in, did you at any point in time look into those matters to see what they did, under whose orders, and who exactly was involved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Before Erdemovic surrendered and gave a statement, I had not been aware of any of that, nor has anyone else been in the intelligence administration. I didn't ask many questions, because later I left for Banja Luka and the whole detachment was transferred there to a new zone of combat operations. And I wasn't interested in that because most of them were on leave at the time. There were only very few soldiers left in the area. And for me, it was a very simple matter. I didn't count on them. My intention and my plan was once they were back from leave to make a proposal to the commander for the whole unit to be transferred to the zone of the 2nd Krajina Corps. Therefore, I knew nothing about that nor do I know anything today, who specifically issued those orders and based on what. This is not an order to the detachment as such, because the detachment was simply not there. There was a group of soldiers who were on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But if you could tell us, when would it have been that you learned what Erdemovic had been involved in? How soon after the events?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Only when he gave those statements, when the media started covering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, how is it, how is it, that you being the head of intelligence, how is it that you didn't know what Erdemovic had been involved in in the field, along with the other group of soldiers that were from that 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I suppose it was one group, first of all; and second, nobody in the Main Staff had ever mentioned anything about Erdemovic's arrest in my hearing, nor was I ever interested in that. I never tried to find out. If I had tried, I would probably have learned. Later I did try to find out some information. And when I did, I found it hard to believe. And investigations, by the way, are not part of my line of work. There are other institutions that are competent and qualified to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you said that you were not interested in that. How could you not be interested in the fact that someone such as Erdemovic and the others executed these prisoners of war, if you want to call them that? Certainly they were unarmed, certainly they hadn't done anything, and there they were being executed. Why wouldn't you, assuming that you were the person who would be issuing directives or suggestions as to how this unit should be utilised, why wouldn't you take an interest in seeing what they were up to or what they had been up to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I made proposals only for those tasks that my organ was in charge of, and that is scouting expeditions, reconnaissance, and intelligence gathering. Second, at the moment when I found out about this from media coverage, I had already submitted my request for early retirement. I had been granted annual leave, and I was placed on call for six months, on stand-by. Sometime in that period I visited the Main Staff as an outsider this time. I was about to retire, and I wasn't really interested. And I talked to another commander who had already volunteered to be retired early, and I asked him whether it was true that they had really participated in that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who was that commander? Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what did you learn from Pelemis?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He told me that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on that information, did you react? Did you do something?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I was not able to react. It was not up to me. It was not my job. The ICTY had already reacted and all the other institutions and authorities had reacted. At that time, I was on stand-by, pending retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, incidentally, had the Office of the Prosecution contacted you, would you have provided this information to them, the information, that is, that you are providing to us today under oath?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go through a couple of -- some other documents. If I can show you what has been marked as P265 or actually has come into evidence as P265. This is -- I'm showing you what is purported to be an intercept conversation. If you could look at it. Do you see your name in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I see that in one place and there's another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. First of all, are you in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. I see one mention of my name. I don't know what it refers to, or rather, I don't know between whom this conversation is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to get at, and it was a poorly phrased question. Were you one of the speakers in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I'm not a collocutor here. I am -- in fact, somebody is saying that some commander ordered something to me, I don't know which commander, and that some order or request would be issued to me. I don't know why this would be true, because I never wrote any requests or orders towards state authorities. I don't know what this is about -- towards MUP, rather. We always contacted only with state authorities. And there is also a reference to some Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know a Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Kovacevic, I don't know even know which Kovacevic this is a reference to. I don't know that we had a Kovacevic in our employ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It also mentions a Keserovic, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Keserovic, I know, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he was from where? Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Keserovic was in the security administration. Whether he was a clerk or something like that, in charge of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At what level was he?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I am not sure. I don't know exactly what his position was, whether it was an administrative assistant, whether they had a section for it or department, whether he was chief of that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he in a corps or was he with the Main Staff? Where exactly -- in which unit was he in?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: At that time, I believe he was in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to briefly go through some other documents. First, I want to show you what has been marked as D194 for identifications purposes, D194/1. Could you please look at this document and first tell us if you know what this document is.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: This is an intelligence brief that we used to submit to the state security service of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if you look at the last -- very last page, it says: "Deputy chief, Colonel Petar Salapura." Would that be you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the date of this report is 8 February 1995, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
