utterances.text: Now, in this particular report -- well, first of all, could you please tell us how is it -- a report like this generated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: This intelligence summary was processed and written by Jankovic. You can see the initials JR, JR at the bottom. He wrote it based on the daily in flow of information processed by analysts, segment by segment. And then a summary is made integrating all this and is submitted to corps staffs and other clients, if I can call them that. This is an intelligence summary that was done every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, is there anything in this particular intelligence summary with respect to the Muslim army that is located in the demilitarised or the supposed or supposed-to-be demilitarised zone of Srebrenica, enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us: What is this information about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Do you mean Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm talking about. That's the only thing I'm interested in at this point in time with this document.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It speaks of the preparation of forces that were in Srebrenica for an offensive scheduled for the spring. It was expected to start in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We can go on to the next document. Let me show you what has been marked for identification purposes as D195/1. And for the ELMO, I'll be referring to page 3, the last page in the English version. But first of all, what is this document, D195 for identification?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: This is also an intelligence summary of the intelligence administration, that is, originating from the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That would be your sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could turn to page -- well, it's 3 in the English version. The third from the last paragraph. Is there any -- do you see what I'm directing your attention to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, the part that you highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just read it here for a second and maybe perhaps we can ask a question or two. It says here: "Muslim propaganda is emphasising alleged VRS operations towards enclaves in the Podrinje region. They have started occupying UNPROFOR checkpoints in the Srebrenica area, while in the Gorazde area on the Gorazde-Ilovaca road, they are using UNPROFOR vehicles to manoeuvre forces and transport materiel and technical equipment, which all indicates that they are preparing offensive operations from the enclaves." Do you see that portion, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, one may think that this particular paragraph is propaganda in and of itself, that is, Serbian propaganda. Would that be correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think the latter part of the question, Your Honour, focused the gentleman in the right area. I can go about it in a different way. I can rephrase. I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But -- well, I don't think this document is relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's going back far from that attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. If -- as Your Honour may recall two weeks ago or last week, they're all blending in these days, last week, we had a witness who indicated that he had been receiving information about an offensive from the Muslims coming from Srebrenica. Now we see that we have intelligence reports here stating the same. So, one, it verifies that that individual who was a combat -- he was a commander, battalion commander on the ground had this sort of information or would have had this sort of information. Secondly, the Prosecution has made a major offensive, if I could call it that, regarding attacks on UNPROFOR checkpoints. And here we see now a document being generated by the intelligence office or intelligence sector of the Drina Corps which says that the Muslims are, in effect, starting to occupy UNPROFOR checkpoints and they're using their vehicles. So we seem to be getting some mixed information, and I'm merely trying to establish that this information was known at the time to those who were on the ground. So I'm trying to put it in perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the long rambling argument. The last witness could have been asked about whether or not he attacked the UNPROFOR checkpoint because there was Muslims there. He was not asked the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not the point of the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All these long arguments telling the witness about, you know, what he's interested in, it's inappropriate, it's not relevant, and the question is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I indicated that I was willing to withdraw the earlier question and rephrase. And then I was invited to give an explanation and I gave an explanation. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, with -- could you please tell us from looking at this particular paragraph what exactly are you trying to say? Because I noticed at least it has your name at the bottom, Deputy Chief, Colonel Petar Salapura, so one might assume that you're competent to elucidate on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, vague. It speaks for itself. Do we need to have this man repeat what he's already said? If he has some specific question about what's said, I think that's appropriate. But "please, elucidate on this matter," this is not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I'll ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was this information true or false? In other words, was it created for the purpose of providing false information to the VRS army of the Main Staff, the Main Staff of the VRS army? I know, it's a silly question, but I've got to ask it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: How on earth? I don't know what to say. Whoever has been in the business that we were in wants to get to the truth as much as possible. The truth and the real information is our main goal. And it would have been a big mistake if our organ has engaged in disinformation. This piece of information we received on a number of occasions. There may be another explanation, however. The enemy may have tried to plant some disinformation on us; however, this particular report was later confirmed because Zepa was under the same command as Srebrenica, and an attack was indeed mounted against the building of the Main Staff. I believe it was in the end of June. I cannot vouch for the date now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me show you another document that we received from the Office of the Prosecution. And this has been marked for identification purposes as D196. Just for the sake of time and for the record, it says that it's 10 June 1995. Sir, is this another intelligence report from you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we could look at the second-to-last paragraph, that would be on page 2 in the English version. It says here: "Muslim forces in Gorazde (81st Division), in Srebrenica (28th Division) enclaves have raised their combat readiness to the highest level and strengthened their forces at the forward line. They are planning to carry out offensive actions in order to insert troops behind our lines and among our ranks." This was dated 10 June 1995. Sir, to the best of your knowledge was this information accurate at the time you put it into your intelligence information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I believe it was true, it was accurate, otherwise it wouldn't be featuring here. That was the information that was available to us. I cannot tell you where it had come from. It was a long time and I don't have the original primary documents, but it must have come from more than one source. Because what you find in this report is in the form of an assertion, concerning planning and intent, so it must have been accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us when you left or retired from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I cannot give you the date now. I don't have my papers with me, but it was in 1996. I cannot be more precise, but I left on my own initiative, on my own request, a request for early retirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A small correction. I know it's getting late, but JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. Thank you. Wrong army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: VRS.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, you should have corrected me, Mr. Salapura. Okay. Thank you. So it was sometime in 1996. Now, could you tell us the reasons for retiring in 1996. Were there any particular reasons other than perhaps old age, if I can be so forward?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, it was not because of old age. I had personal reasons and I had announced my intention to retire early a long time in advance. I had told General Tolimir while the war was still raging that I intended to leave as soon as it was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I have another document from the Prosecution. I just wanted to get your input on this, and this has been marked for identification purposes as D198.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I apologise to Madam Usher for having to travel back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this document, sir, it would appear is a -- an article in a magazine from the RS. And in here it has your name and it states that in essence, for lack of a better term, you were fired, terminated, from your position. That could be found on page 3 in the English version. And it states and I'll just read it for the record, the second paragraph, a part of the second paragraph on page 3: "However, the RS political leadership ended the longstanding disagreements with the military top without a real and objective understanding of its causes and, even more important, without finding the most suitable solutions which would ensure the continuity of the army and the defence of the Serbian people." And then it goes down and it says that a decree was issued by Biljana Plavsic on the retirement and termination of active duty and it goes on and names you, Colonel Petar Salapura. So my question is: Were you terminated by Biljana Plavsic when apparently she was trying to re-organise or adjust the RS, as is suggested in this particular article, D198 for identification.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, Milutinovic wrote this. I don't know based on what, but it's not true. Nobody retired me. I retired early on my own request, and I was the first one to do so in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And since your retirement, where have you been living?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to thank you very much for answering all of my questions. Perhaps Mr. Stojanovic has some questions and I'm sure the Prosecutor may have some as well as the Judges. If you could be as forthright and frank with them as you have been with him, I would appreciate it very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Salapura. I will try to focus on that part of the examination-in-chief which was in relation to P507, which is the logbook of the operations duty officer and I do have some questions arising from that. First of all, I wanted to ask you: Do you know Dragan Jokic personally?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we ever met, actually. If we ever saw each other anywhere, I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You have no direct personal knowledge of ever having had any personal contact with Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, we never had any contact. We might have passed each other, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you P507 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been used before, Your Honour. For the sake of the transcript, let me say that the page we will be looking at is ERN 02935744.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is just one page from a logbook kept by the duty operations officer of the Zvornik Brigade. This is a document, or rather, a logbook, that chief of staff Dragan Obrenovic, when he pleaded guilty, submitted to the OTP. And this is a document that has been used here. Can I please draw your attention to the last passage of the text. As stated before it reads: "Colonel Salapura called - Drago and Beara to report to Golic." Okay. Up here, if you could just look at the date, 14th of July, and then it says: "Jokic." According to Mr. Obrenovic's statement, this was added by him. And then further you have notes taken by the duty operations officer. My question to you is as follows, just to elaborate on something that you have already said: Am I right in stating that you don't in fact remember having had any communication at all on the 14th of July in the morning hours with the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, I did communicate with them on one occasion, in fact. Now, whether it was me personally or perhaps I delegated this to someone, whether it was to Obrenovic or someone else, there was this piece of information that we received. This is something that I still remember. It said that there would be a counter-offensive, a counter-attack, launched from the direction of Tuzla. I'm not sure exactly where from. This is in the Zvornik Brigade zone, and I can't remember off the top of my head exactly along which axis. But I do know that this information was classified as urgent and I asked to have it conveyed. Whether it was myself or perhaps one of my analysts, it's hard to remember now. That's one thing. And another thing that we received in relation to the Zvornik Brigade, something that struck me as noteworthy at the time, whether it came in on the 14th, the 15th, I can't really remember, however, it was either of those two days. I'm not sure for how long the operations had gone on for down there, whether it was during the same offensive, the same attack, the information about an attack by the Muslim units, units of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on an anti-aircraft gun and many people were killed and wounded. This was a result of electronic surveillance. That's how the information was obtained. And it was obtained directly from a Muslim source. These two bits of information, to the best of my recollection, that's what I talked about. How they were monitored and how they were being monitored, well it has been nine years after all. I can't remember any specific details of the situation, but this is what I do remember. And who it was forwarded to, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But in terms of what this report says, this wouldn't lead you to conclude that you took part in anything like this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, I don't see how this makes sense and I can't relate it to anything. It's impossible for me to say. It may as well have been the case, but I can't say what it's about. I can't. I don't know. If you look at it, you see what it says. And I don't know. I can't make any sense of it, why anyone would call Golic or why Drago would, but I don't know, as I said. I'm not -- I simply don't remember. What can I do?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we have information that there was a hill above the Standard barracks where the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade was. There was a radio communications centre that was used for communicating with the duty operations officer at the brigade. Is it possible that a communication like this, a message like this, was relayed to the duty operations officer at the radio communications centre and then this duty officer merely conveyed this message to the duty operations officer further down and for the message not to be conveyed directly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I'm not sure which system they used in the brigade. I simply don't how messages were forwarded, whether their lines of communication were fully functional or not. I can't say exactly how they went about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase it this way: Do you think it would have been possible for this kind of message to first be relayed to the radio communications centre and then that they forwarded this to the duty operations officer, so the communication was not done directly, but rather, the officer up there was told to convey this message to another man to get back to such-and-such a person, and then the duty operations officer went back to the brigade with this bit of information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been entirely possible, why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's already answered. He doesn't know how it worked. So I think that's asked and answered and just keep asking the same question is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And by the way, Mr. Stojanovic, I think the question is very speculative, because that person really doesn't know the communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just another question, Colonel. What about infantry unit -- brigades, did they have a reconnaissance and sabotage detachments within their composition?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: They were supposed to have those. Some did and some didn't. For example, the command of the Drina Corps was supposed to have a platoon and then a detachment, but it never had either of those. Whether a specific brigade had any or not, I really can't say. But all in all, those units, generally speaking, in the Army of Republika Srpska only very rarely got involved in any special missions. More often in combat missions and activities. And they, as a rule, suffered very, very high casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So these units, wherever they existed, would have been subordinated to the commander or to the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: To the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: They would have been attached to the staff itself, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a unit attached to the staff and it was subordinated to the chief of staff. He was the one who decided on the unit's involvement, obviously, and I'll repeat this. The intelligence officer from the brigade would make proposals for the use of that unit and reconnaissance and sabotage. If the chief of staff grants his approval, then that's how it's going to be. But as a rule, those units in 99 per cent of the cases were either used as some sort of reserve by the commander or the chief or used directly in combat operations as some sort of an assault unit perhaps. But they didn't have any other units and those units were not informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. These are all the questions that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We are almost approaching the time for a break. Could we break first and continue, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to start with just asking you a few questions, and you'll notice we repeat many of the same topics, so bear with us and our repetition. I hope to have you out by our 7.00 deadline, but we'll just have to see how it goes. You spoke about intel officers and their relationship to recon units. I take it you were speaking of brigades and corps and Main Staffs. And what you were telling us that it was the intel officer's job to propose to the commander how those units were used. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it worked that way in the brigade and in the corps and in the Main Staff in terms of -- well, the 10th Sabotage Unit for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it was really the commander that made the decisions on how to use the people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Absolutely, he approved or failed to approve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he was the one that would be responsible for that unit's use and what they did?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The sole command and the right to command was held by the commander and the chief of staff, in his own sector. Chiefs of services and chiefs of the different branches had no authority to exercise command, except within their own administration and unit, their assistants, their administrators, that's in terms of everyday activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that applied to security as well as intel officers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. It also applied to security officers, but security officers had their own methods that they applied. Those were also approved by the commander. Those were two different areas, so to speak. Maybe if we look at military police units, they had a higher degree of autonomy when deciding on the possible unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But a security officer would recommend how the military police would be used, and the commander would decided to take that recommendation or not and he would provide the orders for the military police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, also in going back to the intel model, once the commander makes a decision on how to use, in your situation, the recon platoon, is -- would the intel officer be responsible for seeing to it that the commander's orders were carried out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. He would be the one who would monitor the entire implementation and get involved in preparing a specific unit for a specific task. He monitors the entire course of implementation and he is responsible for the orders to be carried out pursuant to the commander's order. He has been trained for that and he is the most qualified person or should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He should know most about the orders that the commander has issued since he's likely proposed them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in that context, would the -- well, the intel officer in the context of the recon platoon be able to pass on orders to the recon platoon that were consistent with the commander's original intent?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand. What do you mean by passing on? Passing on the commander's order, the order that came from a brigade commander, for example, to pass this on to the commanders of the recon platoon or the chief of staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what I mean, pass on the orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Passing on the orders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as a -- basically as a conduit for the commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, the commander could go directly to whoever or could decide to go through the intelligence officer or the chief of that particular unit. This could be transmitted orally in the eventuality of war or in emergencies, or he could do it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In a war situation, let's say with a recon platoon, when the intel officer makes a proposal, the commander supports it, issues an order be it verbal or written, and then the intel officer passes on that order to the recon unit but keeps in touch, and as you've said helps make sure that those orders are carried out. What kind of communication does the intel officer have with the recon unit to make sure those orders are carried out the way the commander intended? What kind of directions, for example, would you expect the intel officer to give in that situation to the recon unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He is the qualified person who agrees on all the details. He monitors the whole thing until the task has been implemented. He looks into whether the men have been trained for such a task, if there had been enough time, whether they have all the equipment that's necessary to carry out a certain task, he considers the nature of the task and the risk entailed. He considers how the unit will carry out a certain task, because now the commander of that recon unit based on the task that has been assigned must take his own decision in his own area of activity. And he reviews this decision with the chief of the intelligence organ thoroughly. Because the objective is to have the task carried out and to keep the casualties down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the situation -- let's go to a real-life situation of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. We have heard evidence here that on about, I believe, the 9th or 10th of July when the fall of Srebrenica was anticipated, the VRS command was able to bring in Mr. Pelemis and a certain number of his members from the 10th Sabotage Detachment. And were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I learned about that, that they had taken part in fighting on the 12th in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you -- you knew that the 10th Sabotage Unit had a base in Vlasenica and one in Bijeljina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you -- were you aware that General Krstic has used the guys in Vlasenica on other operations when the need arose, in June for example?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was an attack against the command post, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did General Krstic, was he able to get that 10th Sabotage Unit and put them to work in the defence in that campaign or that skirmish or battle?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I am not sure which task he assigned to them precisely. I was in Banja Luka at the time, and I was not familiar with the situation on the ground. Because the unit had been subordinated to the command, but it was not within the competence of the Main Staff, not that section anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Srebrenica, I'm talking about another -- something else in June. You talk about it, it was an attack on a command post.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, if that's what we're talking about. That was supposed to be in late June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that you went to Banja Luka for this some kind of treatment in late June.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were obviously aware of the situation in the Srebrenica enclave and the Zepa enclave as it was developing through the spring of March, April, and May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This was a potentially volatile situation. The communication between Zepa and Srebrenica was causing problems to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that earlier that year President Karadzic had issued a directive to make life impossible for the Muslims in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this the first time you've ever heard of it, is now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Going back to Srebrenica, as we build up that problem that you're aware of in May and in the end of May, were you aware of the Drina Corps operation to attack and remove a Dutch operation -- observation post in the area of Zeleni Jadar in the south of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: First I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're not aware -- you didn't participate in any intel analysis or any intel regarding that what I believe was one of the first significant attacks on the enclave by VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the operation that the 10th Sabotage Detachment did a little earlier that year when they went through some tunnels to get to Srebrenica and fired some rockets?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was an operation proposed by you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you're not aware of the operation regarding Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, there was obviously an operation to attack the Srebrenica enclave, the attack we know began on the 6th of July, the attack plans are dated a little earlier than that in the first week of July. Were you involved in the intelligence, analysis, and preparation for the attack on the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. At the time I was in Banja Luka. And I was not involved. I didn't even know that a decision had been taken, nor was I aware of the time frame. It was only later that I found out from the public media. The information I received in Banja Luka in terms of intelligence reports concerning that part, the beginning itself, and that early part I knew nothing about that. But it was immediately in the media, so that's how I found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It would appear from the reports that we see, May and June, that you were probably one of the most knowledgeable people in the Main Staff regarding the situation inside the enclaves and the Muslim forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was not the most knowledgeable person. Perhaps the body itself, the organ, the analysts, and those people who processed this information directly. We continually monitored the situation in Srebrenica ever since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was your best analyst that knew the situation the best at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Karanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your other analysts' names?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Radislav --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That's all. That's all. Unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They never called you or consulted with you while you were in Banja Luka on this major operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I think once the decision had been taken, it was not allowed for them to inform anyone. And I was not interested. I'm not sure if they knew themselves. You know if you have a commander or a chief of staff or the head of sector requests all possible information on Srebrenica or on the general area, then within ten minutes they receive the requested information. There are maps, of course. Maps are updated every day. One of the officers is in charge of updating maps on a daily basis. Therefore, the operation organ, the staff always keeps these maps in the operations room, and whatever information they request in terms of intelligence is always forwarded to them. I'm not sure about the level at which this operation took place, whether it was corps level or Main Staff level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said something and maybe you didn't mean it, but you said you weren't interested. And this was a significant event, the enclaves, the attack on the enclaves. You had written reports about it. You must have been interested. Did you -- or were you not interested?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: You mean who made the decision and how the decision was reached? I'm not sure what reason I could have had to be interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So from what you've told us you come out of your health retreat because of an opportunity to gain information in Belgrade. Is that right, something like that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I did not come out of my retreat. I was still in that same situation. My health problems continued. I simply went to Belgrade under the effect of palliative injection for my spine. I went there to be briefed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you first hear about this Belgrade thing from? And let's start, who within your own army told you about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It was not within the army. It was one of my operational contacts from Banja Luka. I don't know which one of them it was among the four or five who existed. We had communications, telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is what we would call a source, a sensitive source, that you had that provided you with information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't -- I don't think they heard you when you said "moromor" or something like that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't need the names of -- certainly of sources here. We understand that. But can you tell us, was this source a civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I think that is irrelevant whether it was a civilian or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand you don't want to give anything that might identify the source. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, did you tell Mr. Tolimir that you got this information that you wanted to follow up on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was aware of the initial information, even before. The staff was aware of it, too. But to give him more details, I simply could not get hold of him. He was in Zepa and he learned the details later. There was no telephone communication with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Clearly some superior approved your trip to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: This trip did not need to be approved by anyone. I could approve myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So no one approved it, no one knew about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: In that specific case, I cannot tell you -- it's not that nobody knew. Of course somebody knew. But there is a certain plan of activity involved, a plan of my activity, which was of course known to Tolimir, in the operational sense that applied to everyone. But the exact date, whether it would be today or tomorrow did not depend on either him or me; it depended on the call that I was supposed to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. When you went -- you went actually to the city of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you inform the VJ authorities that you would be in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, why would I inform anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, weren't you a member of the VJ? Weren't you being paid by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. No. I was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. And payment arrangements were settled and agreed at the level of their leadership. I received my salary in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Weren't you being paid from Serb sources through the VJ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, financial officers brought money probably from Yugoslavia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we've seen most of the senior VRS officers were -- had what's been referred to as shadow promotions, that when we were promoted in the VRS they were also promoted to the same rank in the VJ. In fact, we've heard that before VRS officers initially would agree to go to Bosnia to fight the war, they wanted to make sure their Yugoslav careers stayed intact, so that even though they were working for the VRS, they were still being promoted by the VJ. Wasn't that the way it worked?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just interject here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps my memory is failing, which is possible, I don't recall hearing this information. This is kind of the first time. Now, I could be terribly wrong on this in this particular case. I'm not saying that perhaps it's not accurate, but I'm just saying I don't recall hearing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think that really matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas -- Mr. McCloskey, put this information into the form of a question. Ask this witness whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Isn't that the way it was working?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That was the job of personnel organs through the 30th Personnel Centre. That was their area of competence. It's true that it functioned that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So most officers in the VRS got a -- promoted in the VJ when they got their promotions in the VRS. In fact, many of them have retired to Belgrade now and are receiving pensions. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I think that those were fictional promotions and retirements for the purpose of justifying these outlays, but that is a question that would be more properly asked of this personnel centre and higher authorities. That's not my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I have heard it described as fictional or shadow promotions. But my question is: Were you getting those same fictional or shadow promotions that the others were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I did, but in Republika Srpska. What exactly the 30th Personnel Centre wrote about it, how they put it down on paper, I couldn't tell you because I didn't see their papers. And I was promoted before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you have any contact with the authorities of Yugoslavia, either the army or the police, during this short trip there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I had with the police at the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we also see that you have -- from your reports that you shared, your reports with the Bosnian state security service, the MUP, the various corps, and the Main Staff, so you had detailed dealings with at least the state security and the MUP in Bosnia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, we did not have any contact with the MUP. We sent our reports only to the state security administration, not to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: SDB?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I would guess you would have had some contacts over in Yugoslavia with those state security services? I'm not going to get into that, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I had contacts with many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And why did you decide to leave Serbia and go back to Bosnia on this trip?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it was the last part that -- I guess I don't object to it at this point, but I thought it was with respect to going -- never mind, Your Honour. I'll just sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not that heavy, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was your work done? Why did you pick the time and date that you did to go back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I came from Bosnia to finish that business. I did that and went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so what day did you leave Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: On the 12th, the evening of the 12th. The same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how far did you get that evening before you stopped to rest?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I went up to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's just right up on the border between Bosnia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had obtained this very valuable information about when the Croat offensive would start. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that what was called Operation Storm, I think, by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did that operation actually start? When did they start shooting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you the exact date now. I don't remember it. I think, according to the information I received, it was supposed to start on the 1st, but it was postponed by a couple of days. It started on the 3rd or the 4th, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the information; I'm asking you when it actually started.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I told you I can't tell you the exact date now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just roughly then.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the 3rd or the 4th, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What month?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're a little bit stuck in July in this case, so we need to make sure we know the months that we're talking about. And I don't want to get into this in detail, but I think we know and history knows that many innocent Serbs were killed in that offensive. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Probably. This Tribunal knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- so this information you had was extremely valuable, it could save lives. Did you stop at the East Bosnia Corps in Bijeljina, where there were secure communications?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to get off a secure, coded Teletype to Han Pijesak or Pale or wherever your superiors were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I sought to establish direct contact with either Tolimir or with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the other name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And only based on their answer would I be able to draw up a written report with details included.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter -- they heard Tolimir, but they didn't hear the name of the other person you were trying to contact.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The commander. The commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who went with you to Belgrade? So who was with you on this trip?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Only the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So had you been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Bijeljina to Belgrade, I only had the driver with me. And up to Bijeljina, there were two more officers with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, sorry to interrupt. Here in the transcript it's still not clear, because we don't have the name of Mladic there. We only have: "The commander, the commander, yes." So would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We just need to make clear for the written record, the commander you wanted to get a hold of was General Mladic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so let me just -- who did you go from Banja Luka to Bijeljina with when you went -- when you were going to Serbia, going to Belgrade? Did you have a driver?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I had a driver with me and two officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were their -- what were the names of the driver and the two officers? And if you want to go into private session for that, we can.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know why -- in fact, I don't quite understand what a private session means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It just means that it doesn't go out to the public. I don't mean anything by it. You just have that opportunity if there's some sensitive information you have, it's the Court's discretion to allow that or not. I'm sure victim and witnesses has explained that to you. In any event, can you tell us the names of the three people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I can. One of them was Mirko Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could get the rank and the unit so we can distinguish who they are.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was a lieutenant in reserve or not. You have to take my word for it, I cannot remember. I think he was a reserve lieutenant, but he was an information technology specialist, a software programmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Another one was Braco Erceg, also reserve lieutenant, programmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the driver?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: And the driver was Radan -- I cannot remember his last name. He was from Bijeljina. Was it Kovacevic? At any rate, he has a nickname of Brdjak, B-r-d-j-a-k. I believe his last name was Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who -- did anyone go with you from Bijeljina to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Only the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you came from Belgrade to Bijeljina, only the driver or did you have anybody else with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Only the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So from Bijeljina down towards the Bratunac area, if you had been in an accident or been attacked and killed, that information would have gone with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were at the East Bosnia headquarters, were you able to become acquainted and updated about the situation around Srebrenica on -- and this would have been I guess the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you heard that Srebrenica had fallen on the 11th of July, the day before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard of it in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you were at the Bijeljina headquarters, weren't you curious to find out from the duty officer, from the intel officer, from the commander, from anyone how things were going down there. I mean, this was your area, this was your army.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know why I would be curious. Srebrenica was taken over; end of story. For me as an intelligence officer, it was the end of story. At the moment our units entered Srebrenica. The entire intelligence work in that area was over and the service was no longer interested in Srebrenica; it was now interested in Tuzla and the possible counter-attack. Our electronic reconnaissance and our entire activity became focused on that. And all the developments in that other area, the columns of people, and everything else that happened was the job of the security services of the command. Our intelligence service no longer had anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Isn't one of the most important sources of intelligence prisoners, prisoner debriefings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is the job of unit intelligence officers from battalion downwards, field intelligence officers and in especially interesting cases, somebody can come down from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that can even go, of course, to the Main Staff, can't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you described earlier how you worked closely with the security branches and you share information. So you share more information with them than they with you, but you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. Our information was available to all organs of the staff on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so the prisoners of Srebrenica would have been a very fertile source of intelligence information for the brigades, for the corps, and for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Not really fertile. I don't know what could be especially interesting about them from our point of view. What would be interesting would be to hear from prisoners from Tuzla, Zenica. Srebrenica was an enclave. There was nothing particularly interesting about it after all those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we'll talk about that a little bit later, but before that let me show you a document. It's P445. Take a look at the B/C/S. It's dated 12 July to the Drina Corps command intelligence section, very urgent -- actually, it appears to be from the Drina Corps command intelligence section, very urgent, to the Main Staff of the VRS intelligence sector. And it's also sent off to the Drina Corps forward command post at Pribicevac, General Krstic personally, and some brigades and Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, chief of intelligence organs for the brigades, also to the MUP of the RS, and the RDB. I want you to take a look at that, if you could. And I want to ask you about whether things were really over in terms of intelligence at that time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read you a paragraph, it's, I think, the second-to-the-last one very near the end of the document. It says: "We have informed organs of the MUP, the RS, and Konjevic Polje about the illegal corridor used by the Muslims of Srebrenica, since it is their task to control the Bratunac/Konjevic Polje road." And incidentally this starts off with a statement that -- from a Muslim prisoner who appears to be retarded and it's a -- comes out, as you can see, under the name of your boss, Zdravko Tolimir. And it goes on to say: "Brigade commands have the duty to fully inform the SJB (public security station) in the area of responsibility." And then it says: "Intelligence organs shall propose measures to be taken by commands to prevent armed Muslims from illegally reaching Tuzla and Kladanj, such as setting up ambushes along the routes they use in order to arrest them and prevent possible surprises against civilians and our combat units along those routes." That's directed to the commands of the Bratunac, Zvornik, Milici brigades. So this is your boss, Tolimir, writing this. Right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Just a minute. "We have informed" -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So there is a role that the intelligence units are playing. And you were playing a role in this work yourself, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. This is OB. Since we are at the level of battalion and light brigades and some other units. On those levels, we were unified. It says: "Organs for intelligence and security, OB."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. And that's -- General Tolimir was in charge of that, and that's intelligence and security. So it's intelligence and security working together?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So there was -- here we have intelligence and security working together. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: As you see from this, there is an exchange of information. The information we receive, we make available to others for their purposes and everybody else was required to make their information available to others. There's nothing special about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And much of this information could have come from captured prisoners, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, it could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So intel officers would have had direct contact with captured prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: They could have had, but I can't say whether a particular officer in the battalion did, in fact, have because he was also the assistant for intelligence and security. This sort of information would have been more interesting to the security service rather than to the intelligence service. If there was an intelligence officer who obtained this sort of information, of course he forwarded information to the security officers or he would perhaps inform the chief of staff and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know that on the early morning hours of 16th July, more Serb young men were killed in battle than probably any other day in the war, partly because of bad intelligence in the area of Baljkovica? Do you want to tell us that that information didn't matter to the infantry units of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: All information is equally important in terms of command. The question is: How much information is there and how do you get the information? But again, I must tell you this is at our rear deep within our territory. And the system is now within the jurisdiction of the security service, as a priority, tracking down those groups, that sort of thing and informing the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You just said that one of your main jobs as an intelligence officer was to get at the truth.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were right there in Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were right there with -- so you had the ability to see the truth, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I told you what I saw. Nothing special was going on back then. I drove through a line of fire in my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you know that Colonel Beara was -- happened to be at the 65th Protection base about the same that you were on the 13th. Did you meet him there or see him there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. No, not then. He wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No one gave you any reports about Mr. Beara being there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. Why should anyone have reported to me about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're an intelligence officer. What Beara was doing would have been of interest to you, wouldn't it, given the relationship between the two?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, for example, if Beara had several hundred prisoners that I think you saw at the soccer pitch, wouldn't you have been interested in the information that those prisoners had?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what effort did you make to find out about the information that those prisoners could be providing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, not me. I was not the one to talk to those prisoners or to seek information from those prisoners. From the battalion down you have a whole system, information is gathered, and finally it is likely to reach the analysts working with the administration. Whatever is needed urgently will be forwarded to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what effort did you make to find out what information was being provided to intel services and security services about those prisoners that were right there in front of your eyes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I didn't do anything at the time. I didn't know about if anyone had gone or not. Later I just wasn't interested in the source. As you have seen, what I receive is processed information, second-hand information. And you can't tell where the information was obtained, where from this source or that source, except in such exceptional cases as this one, what we see written here. You have the battalion, the brigade, the corps, the Main Staff. And everyone processes this information. And what reaches the Main Staff is only what is pertinent to that particular level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were on the ground. You had the ability to find out what might be pertinent by asking a few questions to the officers in charge around you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Again, I was not a unit intelligence officer. It just wasn't my job to go to the soldiers and ask around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There was a commander that you said you met with at the 65th protection area, 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Now, whether he was the commander, I'm not sure who it was. It was either him or -- I can't exactly right now, but yes, the commander. Yes, presumably that's what it says, but he may have been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't make any effort to find out what these prisoners could offer the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: If we take an example, what could possibly be of interest to me? What could I get from those prisoners? What sort of information was it that I would have been able to obtain from those prisoners at the time? At the time none of that was of interest to me. At the time, every minute that anyone from the Main Staff spent -- or me personally as an intelligence officer, would have been wasting time. I focused all of my attention to something entirely different and elsewhere. The Tuzla area, the counter-attack, that's what was essential, and of course the western sector and the forthcoming operation by the Croatian army. That's, as far as I am concerned, on my level as far as the intelligence level further down at brigade level, he is probably interested in every village and every single house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The chief of the 28th Division intel could have been on that soccer field, couldn't he have?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by a helicopter flight, he could have been flown in the day before from Sarajevo, having discussed the upcoming operations, yet you weren't interested in the possibilities of those men on that soccer field. I think that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know, I don't think that that's a helpful comment -- excuse me. Again -- you know, I know it's late, but I don't know that was a question. It was just a comment and it was gratuitous in nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's a comment. I agree with you. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document. It's P865. By the way -- I'm sorry, before we leave that -- the last document, can you tell us where you think Tolimir was as a result -- I'm sorry, can we go back to the other document. It's my fault. Where do you think Tolimir was when he issued this order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say anything about the time or the whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The fact that it says Drina Corps command intelligence section, is that an indication that that's where he might be? I mean, you're the intel officer, can you help us figure this one out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: What that means is he's probably somewhere in the Drina Corps zone. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you tell me.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where. I mean, this would be a mere assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document that I had mentioned before, 865. It's another communication under the name of Major General Zdravko Tolimir. And this has at the top of it -- well, yeah, take a minute to read it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now at the top of this document it says the command of the 1st PLPBR, which we believe is an abbreviation for the Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where is the headquarters of the Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, based on this, I think the brigade was in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Based on what this document says. Personally, I don't know what brigade this was. I suppose it's the Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. That's what it looks like. Would that be -- would that suggest that Mr. Tolimir is in Rogatica on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it says -- this is to the VRS Main Staff, to General Gvero personally. Can you remind us very briefly what Gvero's position was in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Assistant commander for morale and for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And this says: "Accommodations of r/z." What does r/z stand for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it says: "If you are unable to find adequate accommodation for all the r/zs from Srebrenica, we hereby inform you that space" - with a word that they don't know what it means - "has been arranged for 800 prisoners of war in the 1st PLPBR in Sjemec." Now, first of all, let me ask you. There's a word that the translation folks didn't know. So let me ask you if you can help us. The word, "palaca". What does that mean? What's a palaca?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: What that means is there was a room, a large or a small room, or a room like this. Wooden boards were placed there on the ground. And blankets were put there or those thin mattresses to sleep, to put people up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That's what you call pallets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it's the pallet that forklifts use to carry things on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. You lift it from the ground, you put a wooden board in between so there's no bed. There's the ground and then on top of that you place the boards, and that's how soldiers slept, too. But we had -- back there in the army, we had very thin mattresses. It had rubber underneath and tarp on top. You put blankets on top of that and that's where you sleep. This is what you do when you need to put up a large number of people when there are no beds available, that's what you use, pallets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that. Do you know what he's talking about in this first paragraph, what your boss is talking about on the 13th? I think you're in the Bratunac area at that point.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's clear enough what's being sent, a message or a telex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know what's being sent. I mean, aside from this document do you know what he's talking about, from being on the ground and getting information about prisoners, not from this document but from your own personal knowledge of having been there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It talks about putting prisoners up, rather detainees. There were a large number of detainees and there was no room to put them up, no conditions to accommodate them and how those people would be involved in a time to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, were you involved in this potential transport of Srebrenica prisoners to Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How should I have been involved with that? Only if I had my own car to drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't ask you if you went to Rogatica, but were you involved in the organisation and the information related to moving a lot of prisoners to Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I wasn't even aware of it until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It goes on to say: "The 1st PLPBR can guard them with its own forces, and would use them for agricultural work, maintaining the horse, pig, and sheep farm. "If you send them to this sector, this must be done at night, using the brigade transport and troops." Were you aware of any prisoners being sent to Rogatica, any Srebrenica prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the last sentence, it says: "It would be best if this is a new group which has not been in contact with the other r/zs." What does that mean? Why do they want a group that's not in contact with the other Srebrenica prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't like to speculate. I don't know, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know all the prisoners you saw on that soccer field that day were all murdered by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So from your trip to Bijeljina, why did you stop in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: On the way to Bijeljina, no, I was on my way back from Bijeljina and I stopped there to ask where I could find the commander, as I explained some time ago. The command where the military police were stationed, they were in charge of the supplies. And that's why I came by because I thought they should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You drove right by the Zvornik Brigade barracks on your way from Bijeljina towards Nova Kasaba, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you stop there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I don't think so. At least, I don't remember. I'm not sure why I should have. I don't remember having stopped. I don't know what the reason would have been. I don't know. I don't think so. There would have been no reason for me to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you knew a brigade would have had all kinds of communication abilities to find out where Mladic or Tolimir or someone else was, but you chose to go down to Nova Kasaba instead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The same communications equipment was also in Bijeljina. I couldn't get through using the communications equipment. I tried to get through personally to get in touch with them in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So on the 13th when you were in Nova Kasaba, you heard that Mladic was in, where, Srebrenica at the time? Or in the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I was told at that time in the area of Bratunac. That's what I was told to the best of my recollection if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you then drove to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. Right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time did you get to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't define it exactly now. I don't know. It must have been around noon or I can't -- whether it was at 11.00, 12.00, I really can't define the time for you. After all, it's been nine years and this would be mere speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, just 11.00 or 12.00, that's fine. That's just your best estimate. When you were driving from the area of Nova Kasaba, besides the prisoners on the Nova Kasaba football pitch, did you see any more collections of Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Between Nova Kasaba and?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. Between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje, no, I don't remember having seen anything like that, except for the football pitch, that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about the intersection at Konjevic Polje, a warehouse there right on the crossroads?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't notice anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about as you go towards Bratunac maybe a kilometre or a few kilometres from Konjevic Polje towards Bratunac in the little village of Sandici, a big meadow. Did you see any prisoners compiled in a meadow there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. To the left there was a group of prisoners but not many. Perhaps, I don't know, a rather small group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That was past Konjevic Polje on the road to Bratunac, to the left of the road. It was not a meadow exactly, it was just a small clearing. I'm not sure if I noticed anything anywhere else. I can't remember now. But this much I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you got to the Bratunac Brigade, where did you go in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Where specifically? Well, I don't know. I asked about General Mladic. I think it was the duty operations officer that I approached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I asked about the commander's whereabouts and I was told that he was in Srebrenica. And -- yeah, the duty operations officer, but I can't remember. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you in uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You identified yourself as being from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Whether I identified myself or not, these are details. I can't state with certainty whether I did. I probably did, but I can't remember specifically now. These are too many details that you're asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ask the duty officer to acquaint you with the most recent news of the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. Why would I have asked him? It was not his duty to inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were driving in an area where you must have known there were thousands of Muslims running loose. You weren't interested in finding out anything where they might be and what roads might be hazardous and what the situation is along the roadway?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't interested. It was on the way back that I came under fire in my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time did you come back?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know. It's really difficult for me to say, to talk about the exact time, how long I stayed there and how soon I went back. I only stayed for a brief while. How long exactly, it is difficult to say. It may have been in the afternoon, it may have been a bit later. It may have been at 1.00, maybe 2.00. It's really difficult to say. I think it's impossible for me to say right now with any degree of accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
